microtopics.title: Oxidation number, oxidation/reduction and agents
microtopics.badge_reason: The learner must coordinate formal oxidation-state bookkeeping with electron transfer and avoid the common agent-name inversion.
entry_assumptions: Can assign simple oxidation numbers using standard priority rules and can track the same element from reactants to products.
microtopics.inferential_jump: Oxidation number is a formal assignment whose increase corresponds to oxidation and decrease to reduction; an oxidising agent is itself reduced while a reducing agent is itself oxidised.

teaching_path.action: Apply oxidation-number priority rules and require the algebraic sum to equal the species charge.
teaching_path.why_valid: The assignment is a formal bookkeeping convention constrained by overall charge.
teaching_path.output: Charge reconciliation closes the oxidation-number ledger.

teaching_path.action: Track the same element from reactant to product and classify increases as oxidation and decreases as reduction.
teaching_path.why_valid: A direction can only be named after matching the element across both sides.
teaching_path.output: Electron-loss/gain and oxidation-number change are two views of the same bookkeeping.

teaching_path.action: Name the species being reduced as the oxidising agent and the species being oxidised as the reducing agent.
teaching_path.why_valid: Agent names describe the process caused in the partner, not the self-change.
teaching_path.output: Separating self-change from agent role prevents reversal.

misconceptions.wrong_idea: Oxidation number is a literal measured atomic charge, and the species oxidised is the oxidising agent.
misconceptions.diagnostic_prompt: Can resonance/electron sharing make physical charge differ from formal oxidation number, and what happens to the electron acceptor itself?
misconceptions.repair: Label oxidation state as formal bookkeeping; write self-change first, then assign the opposite process as the agent name.

exit_task.prompt: Why is an oxidation number useful even though it is not generally a measured atomic charge?

answer.summary: Its formal assignment rules consistently expose electron-accounting changes between reactants and products.
reasoning: The convention assigns electrons by defined rules.
Changes in the assignments reveal coupled oxidation and reduction.
answer.check: Use the phrase formal assignment and verify the total-charge sum.

oracle.no_numeric_claim: The exit is a bookkeeping explanation; it is closed by reconciling oxidation-state changes and agent roles, not by a measured atomic charge.

microtopics.research_contribution: The conversion preserves the audit correction that oxidation number is formal bookkeeping, and it explicitly separates a species' self-change from the opposite process named by its agent role.

construction_units.decision: Oxidation number is a formal assignment whose increase corresponds to oxidation and decrease to reduction; an oxidising agent is itself reduced while a reducing agent is itself oxidised.

independent_checks.statement: Use the phrase formal assignment and verify the total-charge sum.

predict.prompt: For Oxidation number, oxidation/reduction and agents, decide before the completed route is revealed: Can resonance/electron sharing make physical charge differ from formal oxidation number, and what happens to the electron acceptor itself?
predict.defensible_answer: For Oxidation number, oxidation/reduction and agents, the defensible route is: Label oxidation state as formal bookkeeping; write self-change first, then assign the opposite process as the agent name.

attempt.produces: An oxidation-state ledger that reconciles total charge, identifies which species is oxidised or reduced, and only then names the oxidising and reducing agents.

rubric.criterion: The response treats oxidation state as formal assignment and derives agent names from the effect on the reaction partner.
rubric.evidence_of: It can explain why the electron acceptor is reduced yet is called the oxidising agent, with the oxidation-number direction consistent throughout.

task.prompt: Species A accepts electrons from B. Track the oxidation or reduction of A and B, name both agents, and explain why the oxidation numbers used in the argument are formal bookkeeping rather than literal atomic charges.
givens: Oxidation number is a formal assignment whose increase corresponds to oxidation and decrease to reduction; an oxidising agent is itself reduced while a reducing agent is itself oxidised.

route.ask: If species A accepts electrons from B, what happens to A and B before you attach either agent name?
route.why_this_ask: The initial electron-transfer question creates an unambiguous self-change before any agent label is allowed, removing the linguistic trap from the first step.

route.ask: How can you check that the oxidation-number assignments used in the agent argument are internally consistent with each species' total charge?
route.why_this_ask: The charge-sum check forces the learner back to formal oxidation-state bookkeeping, so the agent conclusion is supported by a consistent ledger rather than a memorised slogan.

reconstruct.differs_from_teaching_path: The expert route assigns oxidation numbers before naming agents; the reconstruction starts with the common reversal that the oxidised species is the oxidising agent and makes the learner build a two-column self-change versus effect-on-partner ledger.

boundary_test.prompt: Why is an oxidation number useful even though it is not generally a measured atomic charge?
boundary_test.answer: Its formal assignment rules consistently expose electron-accounting changes between reactants and products.
boundary_test.confirms: It confirms that the learner can hold self-change, electron direction and agent naming together without reversing any of them.

microtopics.title: Redox classification, displacement and disproportionation patterns
microtopics.badge_reason: The learner must distinguish chemical change from redox and identify split/convergent oxidation-state patterns.
entry_assumptions: Can compare oxidation numbers for the same element on both sides of a reaction and can read reactant-to-product direction explicitly.
microtopics.inferential_jump: A reaction is redox only when oxidation-number bookkeeping shows coupled increase and decrease; reaction labels such as decomposition or displacement do not replace that test.

teaching_path.action: Recognise the chemical reaction without yet calling it redox.
teaching_path.why_valid: Formation of new substances is not sufficient evidence of electron-transfer bookkeeping.
teaching_path.output: Chemical-change classification and redox classification are separate questions.

teaching_path.action: Compare oxidation numbers on both sides and require at least one increase coupled to a decrease.
teaching_path.why_valid: A double displacement can be non-redox, while a displacement can be redox depending on actual state changes.
teaching_path.output: Oxidation-state change is the deciding test.

teaching_path.action: For the same element, map one initial state splitting upward and downward as disproportionation, and two starting states converging as comproportionation.
teaching_path.why_valid: The classification depends on the directed oxidation-state map.
teaching_path.output: Counting how many states appear is not enough.

misconceptions.wrong_idea: Every chemical reaction is redox, and any reaction showing three oxidation states is disproportionation.
misconceptions.diagnostic_prompt: Can ions exchange partners with unchanged oxidation numbers, and are the three states arranged as one-to-two or two-to-one across the reaction arrow?
misconceptions.repair: Run the oxidation-number change check first, then draw the directed state map before naming a special redox pattern.

exit_task.prompt: Why is decomposition alone insufficient to call a reaction redox?

answer.summary: Decomposition describes a reaction pattern, whereas redox requires actual oxidation-number changes.
reasoning: A decomposition can occur without changing oxidation states.
The redox test is independent electron/oxidation-state bookkeeping.
answer.check: List oxidation states before and after rather than relying on the reaction-type label.

oracle.no_numeric_claim: The exit is classificatory rather than numerical; the required evidence is an actual oxidation-number change, not the reaction's surface label.

microtopics.research_contribution: The conversion retains the audit distinction between reaction-pattern labels and redox evidence, including directed oxidation-state maps for disproportionation and comproportionation.

construction_units.decision: A reaction is redox only when oxidation-number bookkeeping shows coupled increase and decrease; reaction labels such as decomposition or displacement do not replace that test.

independent_checks.statement: List oxidation states before and after rather than relying on the reaction-type label.

predict.prompt: For Redox classification, displacement and disproportionation patterns, decide before the completed route is revealed: Can ions exchange partners with unchanged oxidation numbers, and are the three states arranged as one-to-two or two-to-one across the reaction arrow?
predict.defensible_answer: For Redox classification, displacement and disproportionation patterns, the defensible route is: Run the oxidation-number change check first, then draw the directed state map before naming a special redox pattern.

attempt.produces: A before-and-after oxidation-state map that first decides redox versus non-redox and then, if relevant, classifies split or convergent states.

rubric.criterion: The response uses oxidation-number changes as the redox test and uses arrow direction, not the mere presence of three states, to identify disproportionation or comproportionation.
rubric.evidence_of: It can classify an ion-exchange reaction with unchanged oxidation numbers as non-redox and distinguish one-to-two from two-to-one oxidation-state mappings.

task.prompt: Consider a reaction that forms new substances but leaves every oxidation number unchanged; classify it. Then describe the oxidation-state arrow pattern that distinguishes disproportionation from comproportionation.
givens: A reaction is redox only when oxidation-number bookkeeping shows coupled increase and decrease; reaction labels such as decomposition or displacement do not replace that test.

route.ask: Can a genuine chemical reaction occur with no oxidation-number changes, and what would that imply about its redox classification?
route.why_this_ask: A non-redox reaction with genuine chemical change is the strongest way to break the shortcut that new substances are sufficient redox evidence.

route.ask: For the same element, how do the reactant-to-product arrows differ between disproportionation and comproportionation?
route.why_this_ask: The second ask requires arrows between oxidation states, preventing classification of a three-state picture without reactant/product direction.

reconstruct.differs_from_teaching_path: The declarative route separates chemical change from redox before special patterns; the reconstruction starts with every-reaction-is-redox and forces the learner to find a counterexample before drawing split and convergent state maps.

boundary_test.prompt: Why is decomposition alone insufficient to call a reaction redox?
boundary_test.answer: Decomposition describes a reaction pattern, whereas redox requires actual oxidation-number changes.
boundary_test.confirms: It confirms that the learner can resist reaction-name shortcuts and base redox classification on directed oxidation-state evidence.

microtopics.title: Half-reaction balancing and reaction-dependent n-factor
microtopics.badge_reason: The learner must conserve atoms and charge in a declared medium and derive electron-change counts from the specified reaction rather than memorising them as universal properties.
entry_assumptions: Can conserve atom counts and algebraic charge in an ionic equation and can interpret electrons as transfer bookkeeping.
microtopics.inferential_jump: Half-reaction balancing is a conservation algorithm, while n-factor compresses the electron change for one specified redox transformation; neither is valid without the reaction context.

teaching_path.action: State acidic or basic aqueous medium before choosing balancing species.
teaching_path.why_valid: The allowed bookkeeping species depend on the declared medium.
teaching_path.output: Medium is part of the problem conditions.

teaching_path.action: Balance atoms and charge within each half-reaction, then scale so electrons cancel when the halves are added.
teaching_path.why_valid: Electrons are transfer bookkeeping and must not remain in the final net reaction.
teaching_path.output: The final equation must conserve every element and total charge.

teaching_path.action: Derive n-factor from the electron change and stoichiometric role in the specified balanced reaction.
teaching_path.why_valid: The same substance can participate in different redox changes and therefore have different reaction-specific n-factors.
teaching_path.output: Equivalent-mass use is tied to that reaction context.

misconceptions.wrong_idea: Matching atom counts is enough even if charge differs, and every reagent has one universal n-factor.
misconceptions.diagnostic_prompt: Would an ionic equation with equal atom counts but unequal total charge be balanced, and can the same reagent form products at different oxidation states?
misconceptions.repair: Keep separate atom and charge ledgers, and derive n-factor from the actual balanced transformation each time.

exit_task.prompt: Why can a redox reagent have different n-factors in different reactions?

answer.summary: Because n-factor is the reaction-specific number of electrons transferred per formula amount, and that electron change can differ with the product and oxidation-state pathway.
reasoning: Molar mass is tied to the formula.
n-factor is tied to the specified electron-transfer role.
answer.check: Write the reaction or oxidation-state change beside every n-factor value.

oracle.no_numeric_claim: The exit has no standalone numeric n-factor claim; correctness depends on atom and charge conservation plus explicit reaction context.

microtopics.research_contribution: The conversion preserves the audit repair that half-reaction balancing depends on the declared acidic or basic medium and that n-factor is reaction-specific rather than a permanent property of a reagent.

construction_units.decision: Half-reaction balancing is a conservation algorithm, while n-factor compresses the electron change for one specified redox transformation; neither is valid without the reaction context.

independent_checks.statement: Write the reaction or oxidation-state change beside every n-factor value.

predict.prompt: For Half-reaction balancing and reaction-dependent n-factor, decide before the completed route is revealed: Would an ionic equation with equal atom counts but unequal total charge be balanced, and can the same reagent form products at different oxidation states?
predict.defensible_answer: For Half-reaction balancing and reaction-dependent n-factor, the defensible route is: Keep separate atom and charge ledgers, and derive n-factor from the actual balanced transformation each time.

attempt.produces: A balancing checklist with separate atom and charge ledgers, the declared medium, electron cancellation, and a reaction-specific derivation of n-factor.

rubric.criterion: The response verifies both matter and charge conservation and refuses to assign n-factor without specifying the transformation.
rubric.evidence_of: It can explain why H+, OH- or H2O choices depend on medium and why the same reagent may have different n-factors in different redox reactions.

task.prompt: State the final checks for an ionic half-reaction balance in a declared medium. Then explain why a reagent's n-factor must be derived from the specified product or oxidation-state change rather than memorised once.
givens: Half-reaction balancing is a conservation algorithm, while n-factor compresses the electron change for one specified redox transformation; neither is valid without the reaction context.

route.ask: After the atoms have been balanced, what separate charge ledger must still agree on the two sides of an ionic redox equation?
route.why_this_ask: Separating the atom ledger from the charge ledger exposes equations that look balanced by inspection but cannot represent a valid ionic redox process.

route.ask: What information about the actual redox transformation is required before an n-factor can be assigned to the reagent?
route.why_this_ask: The final question makes the learner derive electron change from a stated transformation, which is the only safe basis for an n-factor claim.

reconstruct.differs_from_teaching_path: The expert route balances the half-reactions before discussing n-factor; the reconstruction starts from two shortcuts—atoms balanced means done and n-factor is fixed—and makes the learner use charge conservation and product-dependent electron change to repair both.

boundary_test.prompt: Why can a redox reagent have different n-factors in different reactions?
boundary_test.answer: Because n-factor is the reaction-specific number of electrons transferred per formula amount, and that electron change can differ with the product and oxidation-state pathway.
boundary_test.confirms: It confirms that the learner treats balancing and equivalent bookkeeping as reaction-conditioned conservation procedures.

questions.stem: Species A gains electrons from species B. Which species is the oxidising agent and why?
conditions: Use the formal redox bookkeeping model and reaction conditions stated in the surrounding Core1A construction.

answer.summary: Species A is the oxidising agent because A is reduced while causing B to be oxidised.
reasoning: A gains electrons, so A undergoes reduction.
The electrons come from B, so B is oxidised.
The species causing oxidation of its partner is the oxidising agent.
answer.check: The oxidising agent must appear on the reduction side of the bookkeeping.

questions.stem: The same element begins in one oxidation state and appears in two products, one at a higher and one at a lower oxidation state. What pattern is this?
conditions: Use the formal redox bookkeeping model and reaction conditions stated in the surrounding Core1A construction.

reasoning: One starting oxidation state is both oxidised and reduced in different product portions.
The state map branches upward and downward from the same initial value.
answer.check: Both an increase and a decrease must originate from the same initial oxidation state.

conditions: Use the formal redox bookkeeping model and reaction conditions stated in the surrounding Core1A construction.

answer.summary: Every element count and the total electric charge must match on both sides.
reasoning: Ionic redox equations also conserve total charge.
